title: Where conflict comes from
blurb: Name the typical sources of conflict in projects and diagnose the real source behind a dispute, so you fix the cause, not the symptom.
question: On a warehouse automation project, the operations manager refuses to release staff for testing, two engineers argue about which scanners to buy, and nobody is sure who signs off safety. The sponsor calls it 'a personality problem'. What are the real sources of conflict here?

teach.h: Conflict: when needs, goals or views clash
teach.body: Conflict arises when two or more parties have, or believe they have, incompatible goals, needs, interests or views. In projects it is normal, not a sign of failure. In plain English: people want different things, or want the same scarce thing, and they can't all have it at once. Knowing where conflict comes from lets a project manager prevent much of it and fix the true cause when it appears.

Projects are temporary, so teams are new and relationships are untested. People come from different functions, often in a matrix with two bosses and competing priorities. Time, cost and resources are constrained, so trade-offs are constant. Projects bring change, which some stakeholders resist. And many stakeholders each define success differently. All of this creates friction even when everyone means well.

teach.h: Typical sources of conflict in projects
teach.caption: Nine typical sources, grouped into three families to help you remember them.

teach.body: The operations manager won't release pickers for testing because peak season is coming: resources, driven by competing priorities. Two engineers disagree over handheld or fixed scanners: technical opinions. Procurement insists on three quotes for an urgent part: administrative procedures. Nobody knows whether the safety lead or the site manager signs off the new layout: roles and responsibilities. The sponsor sees bad tempers and calls it personality, but fixing the causes would remove most of the heat.

teach.text: Exam trap: don't grab 'personality clash' just because people are angry. Read what they are arguing ABOUT. Two managers wanting the same engineer is RESOURCES; disagreeing on the go-live date is SCHEDULES/PRIORITIES; not knowing who approves is ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES; one team never told of a change is COMMUNICATION FAILURE.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define conflict: incompatible goals, needs, interests or views between parties.
Explain why projects are prone to it: temporary teams, matrix working, constraints, change.
Name several specific sources (e.g. schedules, resources, technical opinions, roles).
Give a short project example for each source you name.
Show the value: diagnosing the source lets you prevent conflict and fix the real cause.
Conflict = parties with (apparently) incompatible goals, needs or views; normal in projects.
Sources: schedules/priorities, resources, costs, technical opinions, administrative procedures.
Also: roles and responsibilities, personality clashes, goals/objectives, communication failures.
Diagnose the real source; anger often looks personal when the cause is structural.
Many sources can be reduced by good planning, clear roles and a communication plan.

summary: You can now name the typical sources of conflict in projects and explain why projects are so prone to it. You can also look past the symptoms of a dispute to diagnose its real source, in both linear and iterative projects.

A.q: Two project managers both need the organisation's only qualified cyber-security tester during the same fortnight. What is the source of this conflict?
A.why: Competition for the same scarce person at the same time is a resource conflict.

whyNot.0: Nobody disagrees about the technical approach.
whyNot.1: Nothing suggests the managers dislike each other; they want the same resource.
whyNot.3: The dispute is about who gets the person, not about money.

A.q: Two structural engineers on a school build disagree strongly over whether to use a steel or a timber frame. Which source of conflict is this?
A.why: A disagreement between experts about the best technical solution is a conflict over technical opinions.

whyNot.0: No process or paperwork is in dispute.
whyNot.2: Both know their roles; they disagree about the design itself.
whyNot.3: The argument is about the design, not the dates.

A.q: Designs are being approved by two different leads, and each has overruled the other. Which source of conflict is most evident?
A.why: Overlapping, unclear approval authority is a roles and responsibilities problem; a RACI chart would settle who approves.

whyNot.0: Both leads may share the same goals; the issue is who has authority.
whyNot.1: Friction may follow, but the cause is unclear authority.
whyNot.3: The dispute is about who approves, not which design is better.

B.q: A site team needs a replacement pump today, but the finance team insists on three written quotes before any purchase. What is the source of this conflict?
B.why: Organisational rules and processes that slow or block project work are a source of conflict over administrative procedures.

whyNot.0: The pump is available; the barrier is the purchasing process.
whyNot.1: The conflict comes from a rule, not from individuals' personalities.
whyNot.2: Both want the project to succeed; they differ over the procedure.

B.q: Why is it valuable for a project manager to identify the source of a conflict before acting?
options: So the right cause can be addressed
So the person at fault can be named
So the sponsor can resolve it for them
So it can be logged as a formal risk
B.why: Knowing the source means the project manager can treat the cause (for example unclear roles) rather than the symptoms, and choose a fitting way to handle it.

whyNot.1: Finding blame tends to escalate conflict rather than resolve it.
whyNot.2: Most conflicts should be handled by the project manager; escalation is a last resort.
whyNot.3: A current conflict is an issue, not a risk, and logging it doesn't resolve it.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical source of conflict in projects?
B.why: Clear, agreed acceptance criteria reduce conflict by removing ambiguity about what 'done' means.

whyNot.0: Schedules and priorities are a classic source of conflict.
whyNot.2: Unclear roles cause gaps, overlaps and disputes.
whyNot.3: Communication failures are a common source of conflict.

C.q: Marketing wants an app launched before Christmas; the IT lead wants a further month of testing first. Both agree on the features. What is the main source of conflict?
C.why: The disagreement is over timing and what takes priority (launch date versus more testing), so the source is schedules and priorities.

whyNot.0: No dispute about money is described.
whyNot.2: No organisational procedure is in dispute.
whyNot.3: They disagree about timing, not because of their personalities.

C.q: A design change is emailed to the build team but not to the test team, who then fail the product against the old design. The teams now blame each other. What is the root source?
C.why: The test team was never told of the change. The blame between teams is a symptom; the root source is a communication failure.

whyNot.0: The friction is a symptom; it began with a missed message.
whyNot.1: Nobody disagrees about the design; one team simply didn't know it had changed.
whyNot.2: Both teams were staffed; the problem was information, not people.

C.q: On an iterative project, which conflict is most likely to arise at the start of each time box?
options: What goes in the time box
How to close the project down
C.why: Because time boxes are fixed and scope flexes, stakeholders compete to get their priorities into each time box: a schedules and priorities conflict.

whyNot.1: Contract signature is a one-off commercial matter, not a per-time-box conflict.
whyNot.2: Viability is settled in Feasibility, before the time boxes begin.
whyNot.3: Closure happens once, at the end of the project.

reteach.title: Organising a music festival
reteach.question: A small music festival committee is arguing all the time. Before you can calm things down, what are they actually arguing about?

blocks.body: Two stages want the same sound engineer on Saturday night (resources). The headliner's manager wants a later slot than the licence allows (schedules). The treasurer won't approve the fireworks (costs). The licensing paperwork holds up the bar order (procedures). Nobody knows who books the security firm (roles). The chair wants profit, the founders want a free community event (goals). Half the volunteers never got the new site map (communication).

blocks.h: Spot the source, then the fix
head: Argument
Source
Fix

blocks.text: The committee thinks it has a personality problem. Mostly it has structural problems, and each one has a structural fix.

explain.h: 1. What conflict is, and why projects have so much
explain.body: Conflict is a clash of goals, needs, interests or views. Projects are fertile ground: temporary teams, matrix structures with two bosses, tight constraints, change that unsettles people, and many stakeholders with different ideas of success.

test.q: Why does working in a matrix organisation often increase conflict on projects?
options: Teams never meet face to face
test.why: In a matrix, people report to a functional manager and a project manager, whose priorities can compete.

whyNot.2: Budgets can be controlled in any structure.
whyNot.3: Matrix teams can meet in person; the issue is dual reporting.

explain.body: Schedules and priorities (dates, sequence, what comes first), resources (the same people or equipment wanted by several parties) and costs (budgets, overruns, who pays). These are reduced by realistic plans, early resource booking and agreed estimates.

test.q: Two departments argue over which of them should pay for extra security on a project site. Which source of conflict is this?
test.why: A dispute about who pays, or how much, is a conflict over costs.

whyNot.0: No technical approach is being debated.
whyNot.1: Both sides understand the request; they disagree about funding it.
whyNot.3: Both want a secure site; the dispute is who funds it.

explain.body: Technical opinions (experts disagree on the solution), administrative procedures (rules and processes seen as red tape) and roles and responsibilities (gaps, overlaps, unclear authority). Reduced by agreed criteria, explained processes and a RACI chart.

test.q: Which tool most directly prevents conflict caused by unclear roles and responsibilities?
test.why: A RACI chart records who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each task, removing gaps and overlaps.

whyNot.1: A Gantt chart shows timing, not who has authority.
whyNot.2: A risk register records risks, not roles.
whyNot.3: A cost plan sets the budget, not responsibilities.

explain.body: Personality clashes (styles and values that grate), goals and objectives (parties want different outcomes) and communication failures (missing, late or mixed messages). Reduced by ground rules, shared objectives and a communication plan.

test.q: Finance wants a new system to cut costs, while operations wants it to improve customer service even if costs rise. What is the source of conflict?
test.why: The two departments want different outcomes from the same project: a conflict over goals and objectives.

whyNot.0: They are not competing for the same people or equipment.
whyNot.2: The conflict comes from different aims, not personalities.
